r0050: 3. Everyone charged with a criminal offence has the following minimum rights:
r0052: (c) to defend himself in person or through legal assistance of his own choosing or, if he has not sufficient means to pay for legal assistance, to be given it free when the interests of justice so require; ...”
r0054: 23.  The Government asked the Court to dismiss the application for failure to exhaust domestic remedies under Article 35 of the Convention. In that connection, they submitted that the applicant had not raised his complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention either before the National Security Court (*cour de sûreté de l’Etat*) or before the Court of Cassation (*Cour de cassation*), even though, under Article 90 of the Constitution, the Convention formed an integral part of domestic law. They relied on the judgment in Ahmet Sadık v. Greece of 15 November 1996 (Reports 1996-V, p. 1638).
r0055: 24.  The applicant disputed the Government’s argument and submitted that, in his defence before the National Security Court (*cour de sûreté de l’Etat*) and in his written defence submitted to the Court of Cassation (*Cour de cassation*), he had always asked to be given a fair trial. He maintained in that connection that this fair trial was to be understood as the one guaranteed by Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.
r0056: 25.  The Court refers to the domestic-law provisions set out above and observes at the outset that the presence of a military judge on the benches of national security courts (*cours de sûreté de l’Etat*) was expressly provided for by law. It also notes that the applicant did not in any way allege that the legislation had been incorrectly applied. It follows that any challenge to the military judge on the sole ground that he was a member of the armed forces would inevitably have been doomed to failure. Accordingly, such an assertion before the domestic courts could not in any event have enabled the applicant to remedy the situation complained of, since, as the Court has noted, national security courts are established by law (see, mutatis mutandis, no. 9214/80, Cabales, Balkandali and Others v. the United Kingdom, decision of 11 May 1982, Decisions and Reports (DR) 29, p. 176).
r0057: Accordingly, the Court dismisses the Government’s preliminary objection.
r0058: 26.  The Court considers, in the light of the criteria established in its case-law (see, in particular, Çıraklar v. Turkey, judgment of 28 October 1998, Reports 1998-VII, fasc. 94), and having regard to all the evidence before it, that this complaint requires an examination on the merits. It further finds that the complaint is not inadmissible on any other ground.
